artworks.title: Leda and the Swan (after Leonardo da Vinci)
artworks.artist: Cesare da Sesto, after Leonardo da Vinci
artworks.description: Leonardo da Vinci's lost composition of Leda and the Swan, known today through faithful copies such as this one by his Milanese follower Cesare da Sesto, established one of the Renaissance's most influential treatments of the myth. Leda, the Aetolian princess and wife of the Spartan king Tyndareus, stands nude and demure, one arm curving around the neck of the swan into which Zeus has transformed himself to seduce her. At her feet, broken eggshells release the four children born of the union and of that same night with her husband: Helen and Clytemnestra, Castor and Pollux. Leonardo fuses the human figure with the lush fertility of the surrounding landscape, casting the episode less as abduction than as a serene allegory of generation and the cycle of life.

artworks.title: Leda and the Swan (after Michelangelo)
artworks.description: This panel in the National Gallery, London, preserves the composition of Michelangelo's celebrated but now-lost tempera Leda and the Swan, painted around 1530 for Alfonso d'Este, Duke of Ferrara. Michelangelo recast Leda in the powerful, muscular form of his sculpted Night from the Medici tombs, reclining as the swan-Zeus presses against her in an unmistakably charged embrace. The sculptural monumentality of the body, the coiled tension of the pose, and the daring eroticism made the image notorious; the original is said to have been destroyed for its indecency, leaving copies like this one to transmit one of the boldest Renaissance visions of the Spartan queen's mythical union.

artworks.title: Leda and the Swan
artworks.description: Now in the Gemäldegalerie, Berlin, Correggio's canvas was painted as one of a series of mythological 'Loves of Jupiter' and stages the encounter as a tender, luminous idyll set in a wooded riverbank. The picture unfolds the episode across time: at the center Leda sits among her companions as the swan nestles into her lap, while at the sides the bird is shown arriving and then departing. Correggio's soft sfumato, warm flesh tones, and gentle eroticism transform the seduction of the future mother of Helen of Troy into a vision of grace. The painting's later history was turbulent: an owner repeatedly mutilated Leda's head in moral outrage, and it was carefully restored, a testament to the enduring power of the subject.

artworks.title: Leda au cygne (Leda and the Swan)
artworks.description: Held at the Barnes Foundation, Paul Cézanne's Leda au cygne reimagines the ancient myth in the language of early modernism. A reclining nude Leda extends one hand to grasp the beak of the swan, the disguised Zeus who will father Helen and the Dioscuri, while the rest of the composition dissolves into Cézanne's characteristic blocks of muted color and deliberate, constructive brushwork. Stripping away the theatrical eroticism of the Renaissance versions, Cézanne treats the figure and the bird as problems of volume, contour, and pictorial structure, turning the timeless story of the Spartan queen into a meditation on form itself.
